solutions.check: grid rebuilt from the blog's light list (unique); every answer written into it with each crossing agreeing

clue.text: Playing repeats in D flat (10)

indicators.note: letters being played, like notes, come out in a new arrangement

blocks.note: anagram fodder, 10 letters

explanation.surface: A musician runs through the repeats of a piece in D flat.
explanation.walkthrough: The surface welds 'D flat' into a musical key; split it and 'flat' becomes the definition while D joins the fodder.
explanation.definitionFit: Pedestrian prose or playing is flat: dull and uninspired.

clue.text: Kick boat piloted by Pole (4)

blocks.note: a drop-kick of the ball from the hands, as in rugby or American football
a flat-bottomed river boat pushed along by a pole against the riverbed

explanation.surface: Someone kicks a boat steered by a Polish skipper.
explanation.walkthrough: The capital P makes 'Pole' look like a Polish sailor; it is the plain wooden pole a punter pushes against the riverbed.
explanation.definitionFit: A punt is both a drop-kick and a flat-bottomed boat propelled with a pole, as on the Cam in Cambridge.

clue.text: Alumnus about to fill face with duck and game (7)

indicators.note: turned about, so OB reads backwards
BO fills the inside of DIAL

blocks.note: a clock's face is its dial
OB = old boy, a former pupil; turned about to BO and set inside DIAL
a duck is a score of nothing in cricket, shaped like O

explanation.surface: A former pupil stuffs his face with roast duck and game birds.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Duck and game' reads as a menu, but duck is the O and game is the definition.
explanation.definitionFit: Diabolo is the juggling game of spinning a two-cupped spool on a string held between two sticks.

clue.text: TV broadcast with CS Lewis and Lake Poet (9-4)

indicators.note: letters scattered widely, as seed is broadcast, land in a new order

blocks.note: anagram fodder
anagram fodder
anagram fodder, 13 letters in all

explanation.surface: A television programme about CS Lewis and one of the Lake Poets.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Lake Poet' points at Wordsworth or Coleridge; the words split, LAKE going into the mix and 'Poet' standing alone as the definition.
explanation.definitionFit: Vita Sackville-West was an English poet and novelist, author of The Land.

clue.text: Puzzling question consuming theologian with anger (6)

indicators.note: RILE eats DD, holding it inside

blocks.note: to rile is to anger
DD = Doctor of Divinity

explanation.surface: A baffling question eats away at a theologian and makes him angry.
explanation.walkthrough: The container word 'consuming' comes before the thing consumed, with the consumer, 'anger', held back until the end.
explanation.definitionFit: A plain synonym: a riddle is set precisely so the listener is puzzled until the trick is seen.

clue.text: North Georgian resort introduces Pope? (8)

indicators.note: AUGUSTA comes first and leads in N

blocks.note: Augusta, Georgia, home of the Masters golf tournament
N = North

explanation.surface: A northern Georgia resort town welcomes a visit from the Pope.
explanation.walkthrough: The Pope here is Alexander Pope, not the Pontiff; the question mark flags a definition by example.
explanation.definitionFit: Alexander Pope was a leading writer of England's Augustan age of the early 18th century.

clue.text: Day in Rome comes to an end (4)

blocks.note: the Latin word for day, the language spoken in ancient Rome
passes away, expires: the plain English verb

explanation.surface: A day's sightseeing in Rome draws to a close.
explanation.walkthrough: 'In Rome' asks for the Latin word, as in 'dies irae', the day of wrath.
explanation.definitionFit: Dies is the Latin for day, and 'dies' also means comes to an end.

clue.text: Charge million with minimum unit cost to cover? (7)

indicators.note: to cover something is to wrap it up, so the cost lies over and around the M

blocks.note: the lowest price per unit: 1p each, read as I P EACH
M = million, placed after the I

explanation.surface: A levy of a million, with the smallest per-unit fee added to cover costs.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Minimum unit cost' is a price tag, 1p each, with the digit 1 read as the letter I.
explanation.definitionFit: To impeach is to charge a public official with misconduct.

clue.text: Debauched affair in South America involving a performer and boxer (10)

indicators.note: SA wraps round the other pieces

blocks.note: SA = South America, split around the rest
a turn is an act on a variety bill, so a performer
Muhammad Ali, the boxer

explanation.surface: A wild scandal in South America involving an entertainer and a prizefighter.
explanation.walkthrough: A 'turn' is British music-hall talk for a performer or act on the bill.
explanation.definitionFit: A saturnalia is an occasion of wild revelry, after the Roman festival of Saturn.

clue.text: Movement of Duncan Edwards initially demonstrating subtlety (7)

indicators.note: the letters move into a new order
take the first letter of Edwards

blocks.note: anagram fodder
first letter of Edwards

explanation.surface: Praise for the subtle footwork of Duncan Edwards, the Manchester United footballer.
explanation.walkthrough: Duncan Edwards was a Manchester United footballer killed in the 1958 Munich air crash; 'movement' sounds like his play on the pitch.
explanation.definitionFit: Something nuanced shows subtle distinctions.

clue.text: Fail in attempt to extend break? (2,2,3)

blocks.note: collapse or deteriorate, in a common idiom
in snooker a player extends a break by going to pot another ball

explanation.surface: Someone tries to stretch out a holiday and it falls through.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Break' reads as a holiday, but it is a snooker break, a run of scoring shots, kept going by potting balls.
explanation.definitionFit: To go to pot is to decline or fall apart.

clue.text: Boy King embracing female beauty in ballet (3,10)

indicators.note: TUT holds HEN in its arms

blocks.note: Tutankhamun, the boy king of Egypt
a hen is a female bird
a cracker is a stunner, a beauty

explanation.surface: A young king holds a lovely woman in his arms on stage in a ballet.
explanation.walkthrough: In British slang a 'cracker' is anything excellent, including an attractive person.
explanation.definitionFit: A definition by example: Tchaikovsky's Christmas ballet is one of the best-known works in the repertoire.

clue.text: Rest to recover from cold after crossing glens (10)

indicators.note: ONCE spans across VALES, with VALES inside

blocks.note: C = cold, as on a tap
once = as soon as, after: 'once you've eaten'
glens and vales are both valleys

explanation.surface: Advice to take it easy while getting over a cold, after a walk across the glens.
explanation.walkthrough: The surface reads 'from cold' as the illness; it is the plain letter C, with 'from' only a join.
explanation.definitionFit: To convalesce is to rest while recovering from illness.

clue.text: Excellent reason to start with simple tune (3)

indicators.note: take only the start of reason

blocks.note: A1 = excellent, with the 1 read as I
first letter of reason

explanation.surface: A fine reason to begin with a simple melody.
explanation.walkthrough: A1 is first-rate; crosswords routinely read the digit 1 as the letter I.
explanation.definitionFit: A plain synonym from music, where an air is a melody, often a song-like one, as in Bach's Air on the G String.

clue.text: Storyteller’s article culled from Obscure Birds (5,5)

indicators.note: the article A is removed from UNCLEAR

blocks.note: obscure = unclear
the indefinite article, culled from UNCLEAR to leave UNCLER
emus are birds

explanation.surface: A storyteller's article about little-known birds.
explanation.walkthrough: The ’s stands for 'is', joining the definition to the wordplay; the capitals on Obscure Birds make it look like a book title.
explanation.definitionFit: Uncle Remus is the fictional narrator of Joel Chandler Harris's folk tales.

clue.text: One old silly? (6)

indicators.note: letters acting silly fall out of order

blocks.note: anagram fodder, 6 letters

explanation.surface: Asking whether someone is a silly old fool.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Silly' does two jobs: it mixes up ONE OLD, and the whole clue describes the answer, a noodle being a silly one.
explanation.definitionFit: A noodle is old-fashioned slang for a fool.

clue.text: Old Russian soul and wild spirit (8)

blocks.note: in Egyptian belief the ba is the soul
the wild, untamed country, is the bush
in Egyptian belief the ka is the spirit, a person's double

explanation.surface: An old Russian soul with a wild spirit.
explanation.walkthrough: BA and KA are two parts of the self in ancient Egyptian religion, a pair crosswords lean on often.
explanation.definitionFit: Borrowed from Russian, where the word means grandmother; in English it names an elderly Russian woman, or her headscarf.

clue.text: School rebel in form (8)

blocks.note: a comp is a comprehensive, a British state school
to rebel is to rise up

explanation.surface: A school rebel sits in his form class.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Form' looks like a school class next to 'School'; here it is the verb, to make up.
explanation.definitionFit: To comprise can mean to form or make up, as parts comprise a whole.

clue.text: He saw Guinevere, taking look through window (8)

indicators.note: LO goes through the middle of LANCET

blocks.note: lo = look, as in 'lo and behold'
a lancet is a tall narrow pointed window

explanation.surface: A man spies Queen Guinevere by peering through a window.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Saw' is a pun: Lancelot saw Guinevere in the sense of seeing her as a lover.
explanation.definitionFit: Sir Lancelot was Guinevere's lover in Arthurian legend.

clue.text: Ebbing of brown river is to be expected (7)

indicators.note: ebbing water flows back, so TAN runs backwards

blocks.note: tan = brown; ebbing turns it to NAT
the Ural, a river flowing through Russia and Kazakhstan

explanation.surface: A brown river's tide going out is only what you'd expect.
explanation.walkthrough: 'River' is not the flower or banker of crossword tradition here, just a real river named Ural.
explanation.definitionFit: What is natural is what you would expect.

clue.text: Dish of prawns: have most of mine (6)

indicators.note: drop the last letter of PIT

blocks.note: to have someone is to con them
a mine is a pit; most of PIT

explanation.surface: A plate of prawns: eat most of mine.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Have' looks like 'eat'; it is the slang sense, to swindle, as in 'you've been had'.
explanation.definitionFit: Scampi is a dish of breaded Norway lobster or large prawns.

clue.text: Confusion using em dash inverted for example (7)

indicators.note: EG is turned upside down, which in a down clue means read backwards

blocks.note: em is the name of the letter M
dash = flair, élan
e.g. = for example, inverted to GE

explanation.surface: Muddle over using an em dash upside down, for instance.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Em dash' is a printer's term for a long dash; split it into two words, the letter M and élan.
explanation.definitionFit: A mélange is a mixture or jumble.

clue.text: Child really must have name to replace Charlie (6)

indicators.note: to replace is to stand in for, so name takes Charlie's place in the word

blocks.note: in fact = really
N = name, replacing C
Charlie is C in the radio alphabet

explanation.surface: A child simply must have a new name instead of Charlie.
explanation.walkthrough: IN FACT loses its C to N.
explanation.definitionFit: A plain synonym; an infant is a baby or very young child, and in British schools the youngest pupils.

clue.text: Time to pursue game — in which stag has other ideas? (3)

definitions.text: in which stag has other ideas?

indicators.note: a pursuer comes after its quarry, so time is written after the game

blocks.note: RU = rugby union
T = time

explanation.surface: Time to go hunting, but the stag has other things on his mind.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Game' sets up a deer hunt; it is rugby union. The stag's other ideas are mating, not escape.
explanation.definitionFit: The rut is the mating season of deer, when stags think of little else.

clue.text: Confine fish: 50 in river easily sacrificed (10)

indicators.note: the pieces sit in the river

blocks.note: the Exe, a river in Devon, split around the rest
to pen is to confine
a dab is a flatfish
L = 50 in Roman numerals

explanation.surface: Penning fish in a river, where fifty of them are easily lost.
explanation.walkthrough: The Exe is a short river name crosswords use often.
explanation.definitionFit: Something expendable can be given up without much loss.

clue.text: English boozer’s clutching stomach (4)

indicators.note: something clutched is held tight in the middle of the hands, so the boozer holds English inside

blocks.note: a boozer is British slang for a pub, or bar
E = English

explanation.surface: An English drinker clutches his belly.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Boozer' reads as a drinker; in British slang it is also the pub. The ’s means 'is'.
explanation.definitionFit: Both are verbs of endurance: what you cannot stomach you cannot bear, the digestion image standing for tolerance.

clue.text: Spoil Asian language translating a different one (7)

indicators.note: THAI is converted into a new form, its letters rearranged

blocks.note: to mar is to spoil
a different Asian language, Thai, anagrammed to ATHI

explanation.surface: Mangling one Asian language by translating it into another.
explanation.walkthrough: The anagram fodder is not printed: 'a different one' means another Asian language, and Thai is the one whose letters fit.
explanation.definitionFit: Marathi is the language of Maharashtra in western India.

clue.text: Nearly all leaving an American church with suspicion (7)

indicators.note: ALL loses its last letter
what is leaving goes out of a place, so those letters depart from the American

blocks.note: ALL without its last letter
an Alaskan is an American; losing AL leaves ASKAN
CE = Church of England

explanation.surface: Almost everyone quits an American church, eyeing it suspiciously.
explanation.walkthrough: The 'American' has to be one that starts AL, which points to Alaskan.
explanation.definitionFit: To look askance is to look with suspicion or disapproval.

clue.text: Mosul Kurds keeping pet (4)

indicators.note: the words hold the answer inside them

blocks.note: moSUL Kurds

explanation.surface: Kurds in the Iraqi city of Mosul looking after a pet animal.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Pet' looks like an animal; it is the old noun for a fit of pique, as in 'in a pet'.
explanation.definitionFit: A pet, in the sense of a fit of sulky ill humour, is a sulk.

clue.text: Agreed rent around Sussex port in the past (10)

indicators.note: around means surrounding, so the rent is wrapped about the port

blocks.note: yes = agreed
a rent is a tear
Rye, a historic port town in East Sussex

explanation.surface: Rent was agreed on a Sussex port property long ago.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Rent' looks like money paid to a landlord; it is the past tense of rend, a tear.
explanation.definitionFit: Yesteryear, used adverbially, means in years past.
